Why are 252 time steps used to simulate a 1-year price trajectory?

On average, there are about 21 market days per month, excluding weekends and holidays.

This number evenly divides the number of sample paths in the simulation.

The simulation will run 30% faster than using 365 days.

It’s a palindrome.

The correct reason is that, on average, there are about 21 market days per month, excluding weekends and holidays, which totals roughly 252 trading days in a year [1]. 

In quantitative finance, time is typically measured in trading days rather than calendar days. This is because empirical research shows that asset volatility is generated primarily when the exchange is open and trading is active [1, 2]. Over weekends and holidays, when markets are closed, price volatility is significantly lower. As a result, practitioners ignore these non-trading days when estimating historical volatility, modeling price trajectories, and calculating the life of an option [1, 2]. 

This 252-day convention is heavily used when scaling risk metrics. For example, to convert a daily volatility, \(\sigma_{\text{day}}\), into an annualized volatility, \(\sigma_{\text{year}}\), you scale it by the square root of the number of trading days:
\[\sigma_{\text{year}} = \sigma_{\text{day}} \sqrt{252}\] [3, 4].

Does this clarify why we use trading days, or would you like to dive into how we actually build the Monte Carlo simulation using these time steps?
